label: Sayings XXVI–LII
paragraphs: XXVI. To be educated is just this: to learn to will each thing as it happens. And how does it happen? As the one who orders things has ordered it. And he has ordered that there be summer and winter, plenty and want, virtue and vice, and all such opposites, for the harmony of the whole.
XXVII. Keep this thought at hand whenever you lose some external thing: what are you getting in its place? And if that is worth more, never say, "I have suffered a loss."

XXVIII. About the gods, there are some who say that the divine does not even exist; others, that it exists but is idle and uncaring and takes thought for nothing. A third group say that it exists and takes thought, but only for great and heavenly things, and for nothing on earth. A fourth, that it takes thought for things on earth and for human affairs too, but only in general, and not for each person in particular. And there is a fifth group, to which Odysseus and Socrates belonged, who say, "Not a move of mine escapes you."

XXIX. The good and noble man, then, having looked into all these things, submits his own mind to the one who governs the whole, as good citizens submit to the law of their city. And the man who is being educated ought to come to his education with this aim: "How can I follow the gods in everything? How can I be content with the divine governance? How can I become free?" For that man is free for whom everything happens according to his will, and whom no one can hinder. What then? Is freedom madness? Far from it. Madness and freedom do not go together. "But I want everything to turn out just as I fancy, whatever my fancy may be." You are mad; you are out of your mind. Do you not know that freedom is a fine thing and a precious one? But that I should want things at random, and that whatever I happen to fancy should come about: that is likely to be not only not fine, but the most shameful thing of all.
XXX. You should know that it is not easy for a principle to become a man's own, unless every day he says the same things and hears them said, and at the same time puts them to use in his life.

XXXI. But you cannot bear hardship and you are hard to please. If you are alone, you call it loneliness; if you are with people, you call them schemers and robbers, and you find fault even with your own parents and children and brothers and neighbors. When you are alone you ought to call it quiet and freedom, and think yourself like the gods; and when you are with many, you ought not to call it a crowd or an uproar or a nuisance, but a festival and a fair, and so accept everything contentedly.

XXXII. What, then, is the punishment for those who do not accept? To be as they are. Is a man discontented at being alone? Let him be lonely. Is he discontented with his parents? Let him be a bad son, and grieve. Is he discontented with his children? Let him be a bad father. "Throw him into prison." What prison? The one he is in now. For he is there against his will, and wherever a man is against his will, that is a prison to him. So Socrates was not in prison, for he was there willingly.

XXXIII. Do you not know how small a part you are, compared with the whole? That is, in your body; for in your reason you are no worse than the gods, and no smaller. The greatness of reason is not measured by length or height, but by its judgments. Will you not, then, place your good in that in which you are equal to the gods?

XXXIV. When someone asked how a man can eat in a way that pleases the gods, he said: If he can eat justly and graciously, and fairly, with self-control and good manners, is that not also pleasing to the gods? And when you have asked for hot water and the slave does not answer, or answers and brings it lukewarm, or is not even to be found in the house, then not to be angry and not to burst with rage: is that not pleasing to the gods? "But how is a man to put up with such people?" Slave, will you not put up with your own brother, who has Zeus for his forefather, who is a son born of the same seed as you and of the same descent from above? If you have been placed in some higher station of that kind, will you at once set yourself up as a tyrant? Will you not remember what you are and whom you rule? That they are kinsmen, brothers by nature, descendants of Zeus? "But I have a deed of sale for them, and they have none for me." Do you see where you are looking? To the earth, to the pit, to these wretched laws of the dead. To the laws of the gods you do not look.

XXXV. When we are invited to a dinner, we take what is put before us. If a guest told his host to serve him fish or cakes, he would be thought absurd. Yet in the universe we ask the gods for what they do not give, and that when there are so many things they have given us.

XXXVI. When someone asked how a man could be convinced that everything he does is watched by God, he said: Do you not think that all things are joined in one? "I do," the man said. Well, do you not think that things on earth feel what happens in the heavens? "I do," he said. For how else does it come about so regularly, as if at God's command, that when he tells the plants to flower, they flower; when he tells them to bud, they bud; to bear fruit, and they bear it; to ripen it, and they ripen it; and again, when he tells them to drop their fruit and shed their leaves and draw in upon themselves and stay quiet and rest, they stay quiet and rest? How else is it that as the moon waxes and wanes, and the sun comes near and goes away, we see so great a change in things on earth, and their turning to the opposite? But if the plants and our own bodies are so bound up with the whole and feel with it, are our souls not much more so? And if our souls are so bound up and joined with God, as parts and fragments of him, does God not perceive their every movement as his own and of one nature with him?

XXXVII. "But I cannot follow all these things at once," someone says. And who tells you that you have power equal to Zeus? Yet all the same he has set beside each man a guardian, the divinity within him, and has handed the man over to its keeping; and this guardian never sleeps and is never deceived. To what better and more careful keeper could he have handed each of us? So when you shut your doors and make it dark inside, remember never to say that you are alone. You are not: God is within, and your own divinity is within. And what need have they of light to see what you are doing? To this God you too ought to swear an oath, as the soldiers do to Caesar. They, when they take their pay, swear to put Caesar's safety before everything. You have been thought worthy of so many and such great gifts: will you not swear, or having sworn, will you not keep to it? And what will you swear? Never to disobey, never to accuse, never to find fault with anything he has given, never to do or suffer unwillingly anything that must be. Is this oath like the other? There they swear to put no one before Caesar; here, to put themselves before everything.
XXXVIII. "How, then, can I get my brother to stop being angry with me?" Bring him to me and I will tell him. But to you I have nothing to say about his anger.

XXXIX. When the man who was consulting him said, "What I am asking is this: how, even if he will not be reconciled to me, I may stay in keeping with nature," he said: Nothing great comes into being all at once; not even a bunch of grapes or a fig does. If you tell me now, "I want a fig," I will answer, "It takes time." Let it flower first, then put out its fruit, then ripen. The fruit of a fig tree is not brought to perfection suddenly, in a single hour; and do you want to gain the fruit of a man's mind so quickly and so easily? Do not expect it, not even if I tell you so myself.

XL. Epaphroditus had a shoemaker whom he sold because he was useless. Then by some stroke of fortune the man was bought by one of Caesar's household and became shoemaker to Caesar. You should have seen how Epaphroditus honored him. "How is my good Felicio? I am so fond of you." And if any of us asked, "What is the master doing?" we were told, "He is consulting with Felicio about something." Had he not sold him as useless? Who then had suddenly made him wise? This is what it is to honor anything other than what lies within the will.

XLI. What you avoid suffering yourself, do not try to impose on others. You avoid slavery: take care not to be served by slaves. For if you can bear to be served by slaves, you seem to have been a slave yourself first. Virtue has nothing in common with vice, nor freedom with slavery.

XLII. A man has been honored with the tribuneship. Everyone he meets congratulates him. One kisses his eyes, another his neck, and the slaves his hands. He comes home and finds lamps being lit. He goes up to the Capitol and offers sacrifice. Now who has ever offered sacrifice for having desired rightly, or for having felt an impulse in keeping with nature? For we give thanks to the gods for the things in which we place our good.

XLIII. Today a man was talking to me about a priesthood of Augustus. I said to him, "Man, let the thing go. You will spend a great deal for nothing." "But those who draw up contracts will write my name on them." "And will you stand beside the people who read them and say, 'That is my name they have written'? And even if you can be present at every reading now, what will you do when you die?" "My name will remain." "Carve it on a stone and it will remain. But come, outside Nicopolis who will remember you?" "But I will wear a crown of gold." "If you want a crown at all, take one of roses and put it on. You will look smarter in it."

XLIV. And the chief thing: remember that the door is open. Do not be more cowardly than children. When the game stops pleasing them, they say, "I won't play any more." So you too, when things seem that way to you, say, "I won't play any more," and go. But if you stay, do not complain.

XLV. Has someone made smoke in the house? If it is moderate, I will stay; if it is too much, I go out. For you must remember this and hold on to it: the door is open. "Do not live in Nicopolis." I will not. "Nor in Athens." Not in Athens. "Nor in Rome." Not in Rome. "Live on Gyara." I will live there. But living on Gyara seems to me like a great deal of smoke. I go off to where no one will hinder me from living; for that dwelling is open to everyone. And as for the last little tunic, which is this poor body, beyond that no one has any power over me. That is why Demetrius said to Nero, "You threaten me with death, but nature threatens you."

XLVI. This, then, is the beginning of philosophy: to perceive the state of one's own ruling faculty. For once a man knows that it is weak, he will no longer want to use it for great things. But as it is, some who cannot swallow a mouthful buy a whole treatise and set about eating it. So they vomit, or get indigestion; and then come cramps and fluxes and fevers. They ought to stop and ask whether they are able.

XLVII. In theory it is easy to refute a man who does not know; but in the business of life no one offers himself to be refuted, and we hate the man who has refuted us. But Socrates used to say that we should not live an unexamined life.

XLVIII. That is why Socrates, when someone reminded him to prepare for his trial, said, "Do you not think I have been preparing for this my whole life?" "What kind of preparation?" "I have kept safe what is in my power," he said. "How?" "I have never done anything unjust, in private or in public."

XLIX. In what role, then, do you step up now? As a witness called by God. "Come, you, and bear witness for me; for you are worthy to be brought forward as a witness by me. Is anything outside the will good or evil? Do I harm anyone? Have I put each man's benefit in anyone's power but his own?" What witness do you bear for God? "I am in a terrible state, master, and I am unlucky. No one cares about me, no one gives me anything, everyone blames me and speaks ill of me." Is this the witness you are going to bear? Will you disgrace the calling he has called you to, when he has done you this honor and thought you worthy to be brought forward to bear witness in so great a matter?
L. If you want to be well spoken of, learn to speak well; and when you have learned to speak well, try to act well, and in that way you will reap the reward of being well spoken of.

LI. When you go in to see one of the great, remember that another is looking down from above at what happens, and that you must please him rather than this man. So he asks you, "Exile and prison and chains and death and disgrace: what did you call them in the school?" "I called them indifferent." "And what do you call them now? Have they changed at all?" "No." "Have you changed, then?" "No." "Then say what things are indifferent." "Things outside the will." "Say what follows." "Things outside the will are nothing to me." "Say also what you all thought the good things were." "A will and a use of impressions such as they ought to be." "And the end?" "To follow you."

LII. "So Socrates had to suffer these things at the hands of the Athenians?" Slave, why do you say "Socrates"? Say the thing as it is: that Socrates' poor body had to be carried off and dragged to prison by those who were stronger, and that someone had to give hemlock to Socrates' poor body, and that it had to grow cold and die. Do these things seem astonishing to you, do they seem unjust? Is it for these that you accuse God? Did Socrates have nothing, then, in exchange for them? Where, for him, did the essence of the good lie? Whom shall we listen to, you or him? And what does he say? "Anytus and Meletus can kill me, but they cannot harm me." And again, "If this is what pleases God, so be it."

divergences.phrase: ἐπίτροπον ἑκάστῳ παρέστησεν τὸν ἑκάστου δαίμονα
divergences.older: "God hath placed by the side of each a man's own Guardian Spirit" (Crossley)
divergences.lectio: "he has set beside each man a guardian, the divinity within him"
divergences.note: The daimon is rendered as the Lectio Meditations renders it, "the divinity within", so the two books say the same thing with the same words. Epictetus himself says in the next breath that it is "within" (ἔνδον). The subject of the sentence is Zeus, named just before; Crossley writes "God".

divergences.phrase: φεύγεις δὲ δουλείαν, φυλάσσου τὸ δουλεύεσθαι
divergences.lectio: "You avoid slavery: take care not to be served by slaves."
divergences.note: δουλεύεσθαι is passive, "to be slaved for": the maxim is against keeping slaves, not only against making them. The saying is from the collection of maxims Stobaeus passes down under Epictetus's name (Schenkl's Gnomologium, no. 36); it is not from Arrian and may not be Epictetus's.

divergences.phrase: Εἰ θέλεις καλῶς ἀκούειν, μάθε καλῶς λέγειν
divergences.older: "Wouldst thou have men speak good of thee? speak good of them … try to do good unto them" (Crossley)
divergences.lectio: "If you want to be well spoken of, learn to speak well … try to act well"
divergences.note: The Greek plays on one adverb through three verbs: to hear well (be well spoken of), to speak well, to act well. It has no "of them" and no "unto them"; Crossley supplied both. Also from the Stobaean maxims (Gnomologium 7), of doubtful authorship.
